title: Benefit-framing 'This can help...' construction
description: This latent fires on the specific syntactic pattern of a sentence opening with 'This can/will help(s)...' used to state the positive benefit or outcome of a preceding suggestion, typically in advice-giving text about interpersonal communication (e.g., building trust, reducing tension, feeling heard, boosting confidence). It activates most strongly on the bare template itself ('This can help', 'This will help you'), and more moderately on fuller versions that specify the benefit clause (e.g., 'This can help build trust and understanding'). It does not activate on other advice-giving sentences that use different phrasing to convey benefit or rationale (e.g., 'It's important to...', 'Try to...', 'This shows that...'), nor on sentences discussing feelings, validation, or advice content without the explicit 'This can/will help' opener, even if topically similar (trust, empathy, conflict resolution).

title: Formulaic reassurance/affirmation phrases
description: This latent fires on stock affirming phrases that directly address 'you' with formulaic emotional validation, especially the templated openers 'Remember, you are...' / 'You deserve...' / 'You are not alone,' typically delivering messages of worth, strength, capability, or entitlement to happiness. It activates most strongly on the exact scaffolding words themselves ('Remember that you are', 'You deserve', 'You are worthy of') even in truncated or list-like form, and generalizes to fuller sentences combining these same boilerplate affirmations (strong, capable, deserving of love/respect, not alone, enough). It does not activate on general supportive or advice-giving sentences that lack this specific affirmation template—e.g. sentences offering practical suggestions, perspective-taking, or empathetic explanations ('It's understandable that...', 'Try to see things from her perspective') are not the target even though they share a similarly supportive tone, because they lack the direct 'you are/you deserve' affirmational framing.

title: Exclamatory empathetic framing opener
description: This latent fires on short exclamatory phrases that frame or react to the situation just described, typically of the form 'What a [adjective] situation/realization/feeling!' or 'The eternal/age-old/classic struggle/dilemma!'. These serve as an empathetic or evaluative interjection, usually appearing at the start of a response to validate or characterize the emotional weight, difficulty, or universality of the topic before elaborating further. It activates specifically on this templated exclamation-with-adjective-plus-noun pattern (tough, challenging, wonderful, painful, profound, etc.) rather than on the substantive content that follows. It does NOT activate on full declarative sentences of advice, explanation, or validation (e.g., 'It's understandable that you're frustrated' or 'You're not the a**hole here'), even when they express similar empathy, because those lack the short exclamatory 'What a...!' or 'The eternal...!' framing structure.

title: Clarifying follow-up question prompt
description: This latent fires on the assistant's formulaic clarifying question that invites the user to elaborate on their situation or feelings, especially the templated phrase 'Can you tell me more about what happened/what's been going on/how you're feeling?' and close variants like 'What specifically are you referring to/worried about?'. It activates on direct, second-person interrogative prompts whose sole function is to solicit more detail before giving advice, regardless of the topic being discussed. It does not activate on declarative statements, advice, reassurance, or analysis of the user's situation (e.g. 'It sounds like you're feeling...', 'You could say...'), nor on rhetorical or embedded questions that occur mid-explanation rather than as a standalone request for elaboration; it is specifically tied to the open-ended 'tell me more / what specifically' clarifying-question construction.

title: Advice to have an open, honest conversation
description: This latent fires on the recurring advice-column template of recommending that the reader 'have an open and honest conversation' with a specific person (girlfriend, mother, sibling, boss, etc.) about their feelings or concerns, often framed as a bolded header like 'Communicate openly:' followed by the recommendation. It activates most strongly on the near-formulaic phrasing itself (the noun phrase 'open and honest conversation' plus a named interlocutor and topic), rather than on general communication-related advice. It does not activate strongly on related but differently phrased communication advice, such as suggestions to listen actively, use 'I' statements, be honest, set boundaries, or reflect on feelings, unless they specifically invoke the 'open and honest conversation' construction; broader relationship or self-care advice without this exact template activates it weakly or not at all.

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeral token that begins or marks an item in an enumerated list (e.g., '5.', '3.', '2. **'), regardless of the list's topic. It activates most strongly on bare or lightly formatted digits followed by a period, especially in mid-range list sequences, and also fires more weakly on similar numeral markers embedded in bolded or bulleted list formatting. It would not activate on prose sentences without list structure, on spelled-out numbers used in running text, or on list items introduced by bullets/asterisks without a leading numeral, since the key trigger is the digit-plus-period pattern signaling a list position.

title: Suggested self-improvement activity items
description: This latent fires on itemized or bulleted suggestions recommending specific leisure, wellness, learning, or social activities (e.g., 'take a class or workshop', 'try yoga', 'engage in creative pursuits', 'attend events'), typically phrased as bolded imperative headers followed by concrete examples. It activates most strongly on formulaic advice-list entries offering hobbies, exercise, classes, or social gatherings as coping/self-improvement strategies, often in response-generation contexts like 'here are some suggestions'. It does not activate on general advice about interpersonal communication, emotional reassurance, or reasoning about a person's situation/feelings, even when these appear in similarly numbered lists, since the key trigger is the concrete recommendation of an activity/hobby/class rather than relational or emotional guidance.

title: Introductory lead-in phrase before a list
description: This latent fires on short transitional phrases like "Here's why:", "Here are some points to consider:", "Here's my take:", or "Here's a breakdown:" that immediately precede an enumerated list (often starting with "1."). It captures the structural/formatting pattern of announcing that a list of reasons, suggestions, or considerations is about to follow, rather than the content of the list itself. It activates most strongly right at the colon/newline boundary where the numbered item begins. It does not activate on general advice-giving sentences, empathetic statements, or substantive reasoning content that lacks this specific "lead-in phrase + list marker" structure, even if topically similar (e.g. relationship advice sentences without an introductory list phrase).

title: Numbered list item markers
description: This latent fires on the numeric markers that begin enumerated list items (e.g., '1.', '2.', '3.', '4.'), especially when followed by bold markdown formatting ('**') as often occurs in structured advice or reasoning breakdowns. It activates most strongly on the bare digit-plus-period token itself, regardless of what point follows, and appears frequently in texts that enumerate considerations, reasons, or options (e.g., relationship-advice or argument-analysis responses). It does not activate on ordinary prose sentences that make similar evaluative points ('You're not being flaky', 'This is a reasonable expectation') unless they are prefixed by an explicit list-numbering token, so the trigger is the structural enumeration marker itself rather than the semantic content of the point being made.
